Number|Place value.intro: Each digit is worth a different amount depending on its place: thousands, hundreds, tens, ones.
examples: It is in the hundreds place, so it is worth 700. 4738 = 4000 + 700 + 30 + 8.

Number|Sequences.intro: Find the jump between neighbours. Check it works for every pair, then keep jumping.
examples: What is the 5th number? Start at 20, jump +4
The 5th number is 4 jumps after the 1st: 20 + 4 × 4 = 36. (20, 24, 28, 32, 36)

Number|Negative numbers.intro: Numbers below zero are negative. On a number line, smaller numbers are to the left and bigger numbers are to the right.
examples: −6 is further to the left on the line, so −6 < −2.
Start at −4 and jump 10 to the right: 4 jumps take you to 0, then 6 more. Answer: 6.
Find both numbers on the line and count the jumps between them: 3 jumps from −3 to 0, then 5 jumps from 0 to 5. 3 + 5 = 8 degrees.
Start at 5 and count back in 4s: 5, 1, ___
Jump 4 to the left from 1: 1 jump to 0, then 3 more. Answer: −3.

Number|Rounding.intro: Look at the digit just after the place you round to. 5 or more: round up. 4 or less: round down. On the number line, see which end the number is nearer.
examples: 4738 is between 4730 and 4740. The ones digit is 8 (5 or more), so round up: 4740.
4738 is between 4700 and 4800. The tens digit is 3 (4 or less), so round down: 4700.
4738 is between 4000 and 5000. The hundreds digit is 7, so round up: 5000.
Smallest whole number that rounds to 600 (nearest 100)
550. Halfway between 500 and 600 is 550, and halfway rounds up. Numbers from 550 to 649 round to 600.

Number|Roman numerals.intro: I = 1, V = 5, X = 10, L = 50, C = 100. A smaller letter in front of a bigger one means take it away.

Add and subtract|Adding.intro: Line up ones under ones. Add from the right. If a column makes 10 or more, write the ones and carry the ten.
examples: Ones: 6 + 8 = 14, write 4 carry 1. Tens: 7 + 5 + 1 = 13, write 3 carry 1. Hundreds: 4 + 2 + 1 = 7. Answer: 734.

Add and subtract|Subtracting.intro: Start with the ones. If the top digit is too small, exchange 1 ten for 10 ones.
examples: Ones: 3 − 7 can't be done, exchange: 13 − 7 = 6. Tens: 3 − 6, exchange: 13 − 6 = 7. Hundreds: 7 − 3 = 4. Answer: 476.

Add and subtract|Missing digits.intro: Work column by column from the ones. Remember any number carried.
examples: Ones: 6 + □ ends in 1, so □ = 5 (11, carry 1). Tens: □ + 4 + 1 = 8, so □ = 3.

Add and subtract|Checking calculations.intro: Check a subtraction by adding back. Compare by working out each side.
examples: Left: 14. Right: 14. So the sign is =.

Add and subtract|Word problems.intro: Read it twice. Write each step as a calculation, then answer the question that was asked.
examples: 52 on a bus, some get off, 17 get on, now 46. How many got off?
Zara is 8, her dad is 41. How old is dad when Zara is 20?

Multiply and divide|Times tables.intro: Use a fact you know to find one you don't. Division is a times table backwards.

Multiply and divide|× by 0 and 1, three.intro: × 1 leaves a number the same. × 0 is always 0. You can multiply three numbers in any order.

Multiply and divide|× and ÷ by 10 and 10.intro: × 10: every digit moves 1 place to the left. × 100: 2 places to the left. Dividing moves the digits to the right.

Multiply and divide|× and ÷ by 10, 100,.intro: × 10, 100, 1000: digits move 1, 2 or 3 places left. ÷: digits move right.

Multiply and divide|Column multiplicatio.intro: Write the numbers in columns. Multiply the ones first, then the tens, then the hundreds. Carry when an answer is 10 or more.

Multiply and divide|Short division.intro: Start on the left. Divide one digit at a time and write each answer above the line. Carry anything left over to the next digit.
examples: 9 ÷ 4 = 2 r 1. Carry the 1 to make 16. 16 ÷ 4 = 4. Answer: 24.
3 is smaller than 5, so start with 36. 36 ÷ 5 = 7 r 1. Carry the 1 to make 15. 15 ÷ 5 = 3. Answer: 73.

Multiply and divide|Division with remain.intro: Find how many whole groups fit. What is left over is the remainder.

Multiply and divide|Comparing calculatio.intro: Work out each side first, then choose <, > or =.

Multiply and divide|Word problems.intro: With a remainder, decide: do you need one more (round up) or only full groups (round down)?
examples: 28 children, 6 in each car. How many cars?
28 ÷ 6 = 4 r 4. The 4 left over need a car too: 5 cars.
28 eggs, boxes of 6. How many full boxes?

Fractions|Equivalent fractions.intro: Multiply the top and the bottom by the same number and the fraction stays the same size. Follow the arrows: the same × on the top and on the bottom.

Fractions|Simplest form.intro: Divide the top and the bottom by the same number until you cannot go any further. Follow the arrows: the same ÷ on the top and on the bottom.

Fractions|Mixed numbers.intro: A mixed number is a whole number and a fraction. An improper fraction has a top number bigger than the bottom.

Fractions|Compare & order.intro: Same bottom number: compare the tops. Same top number: the bigger bottom means smaller pieces. Counting in fractions: the top changes, the bottom stays.
examples: Same bottom: 5 is more than 3, so 5/8 is bigger.
Fifths are smaller pieces than thirds, so 1/3 is bigger.
1 1/4 = 5/4. 7 is more than 5, so 7/4 is bigger.

Fractions|Add & subtract.intro: When the bottom numbers are the same, add or take away the tops. The bottom stays the same.

Fractions|Fractions of amounts.intro: Divide by the bottom number, then multiply by the top number.

Fractions|Fractions ↔ decimals.intro: Tenths go in the first place after the point, hundredths in the second. Learn 1/2, 1/4 and 3/4 by heart.

Fractions|Word problems.intro: Draw a bar split into equal parts to see the fraction of the amount.
examples: A pizza has 8 slices. Tom eats 3/8. How many slices are left?

Decimals|Fractions ↔ decimals.intro: The first place after the point is tenths, the second is hundredths.

Decimals|Compare & order.intro: Compare the whole numbers first, then tenths, then hundredths.
examples: Tenths: 7 is more than 6, so 0.7 is bigger.
Tenths: 4 is more than 3, so 2.4 is bigger.

Decimals|Rounding.intro: To the nearest whole number, look at the tenths digit: 5 or more round up, 4 or less round down.

Decimals|÷ by 10, 100, 1000.intro: Dividing by 10 moves the digits one place right. By 100, two places.

Decimals|Word problems.intro: Line up the decimal points when adding or taking away, and write the units in your answer.

Money & Time|Rounding money.intro: To the nearest pound, look at the pence: 50p or more round up.

Money & Time|Word problems.intro: £1 = 100p. Add up the cost of everything bought first. Then take the total away from the money paid (for example £10) to find the change.

Money & Time|Telling the time.intro: The short hand shows the hour. The long hand shows minutes: each number is 5 minutes.
examples: 10 × 5 = 50 minutes past, which is 10 minutes to the next hour.

Money & Time|Time problems.intro: Count on in steps: first to the next o'clock, then the rest.
examples: 60 seconds = 1 minute, 60 minutes = 1 hour, 24 hours = 1 day, 7 days = 1 week.

as.intro: Line the numbers up by place value (ones under ones). Add or subtract from the right, carrying or exchanging when you need to.
examples: 7 + 6 = 13: write 3, carry 1. 8 + 7 + 1 = 16: write 6, carry 1. 5 + 6 + 1 = 12: write 2, carry 1. 4 + 1 = 5. Answer 5263.
Exchange across the zeros: 5003 becomes 4 thousands, 9 hundreds, 9 tens and 13 ones. 13 − 7 = 6, 9 − 4 = 5, 9 − 8 = 1, 4 − 1 = 3. Answer 3156.

md.intro: Multiply big numbers in columns. Divide with short division: divide each digit, carrying the remainder to the next digit.
examples: Multiply first: 7 × 3 = 21. Then left to right: 25 − 21 + 6 = 10.

roman.intro: I = 1, V = 5, X = 10, L = 50, C = 100, D = 500, M = 1000. A smaller letter before a bigger one is taken away (IV = 4, XC = 90).
examples: 1000 = M, 900 = CM, 90 = XC, 4 = IV. So MCMXCIV.

round.intro: Look at the digit to the right of the place you round to: 5 or more rounds up, 4 or less rounds down. For 'largest and smallest' questions, find the range of numbers that round to the value.
examples: The hundreds digit is 6, so round up: 39 000.
A whole number rounds to 3700 to the nearest 100. What is the largest it could be?
Numbers from 3650 to 3749 round to 3700. The largest is 3749.

pow.intro: A power tells you how many times to multiply a number by itself: 2 to the power 5 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32. Squares are power 2, cubes are power 3.
examples: 3 × 3 = 9, × 3 = 27, × 3 = 81. That is four 3s, so the power is 4.

fact.intro: Factors divide exactly into a number. Multiples are in its times table. Find factors in pairs: 1 × 24, 2 × 12, 3 × 8, 4 × 6.
examples: Pairs: 1 × 36, 2 × 18, 3 × 12, 4 × 9, 6 × 6. That is 9 factors (6 only counts once).
What is the smallest number that is a multiple of 6 and 8?
Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24 … 24 is also a multiple of 6. So 24.

prime.intro: A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. 1 is not prime. 2 is the only even prime.
examples: Write 60 as a product of primes.

asn.intro: Always: true for every example. Never: true for none. Sometimes: you can find one example where it is true and one where it is false.
examples: A multiple of 4 is a multiple of 8.
16 is, but 12 is not. So sometimes true.
The sum of two odd numbers is even.
Odd + odd is always even: always true.

frac.intro: To add or subtract fractions, make the denominators the same first. Change mixed numbers to improper fractions if it helps, and simplify the answer.

dec.intro: Line up the decimal points when you add or subtract. When you multiply, ignore the point, multiply, then put it back with the same number of decimal places.

famt.intro: To find a fraction of an amount, divide by the bottom number, then multiply by the top number.

place.intro: × 10 moves every digit one place to the left; ÷ 10 moves it one place to the right. × 100 and × 1000 move it two and three places.

money.intro: Find 10% by dividing by 10, then build other percentages from it. A percentage increase adds on; a decrease takes off. For 'price before', work out what 1% is.
examples: After 20% off a coat costs £48. What was it before?

order.intro: Change everything to decimals to compare: 3/4 = 0.75, 2/5 = 0.4, 7% = 0.07. Then order the decimals digit by digit.

examples: Write 0.24 as a fraction in simplest form.

ratio.intro: In a ratio like 2 : 3 there are 2 + 3 = 5 parts. Divide the total by the number of parts to find one part.
examples: Red and blue beads are 2 : 7. There are 14 red. How many blue?

unitc.intro: Find the cost of one, then multiply. To compare packs, work out the price for the same amount, such as per 100 g.
examples: Pack A: 400 g for £2. Pack B: 250 g for £1.50. Which is better value?
A: 50p per 100 g. B: 60p per 100 g. A is better value.

rates.intro: Scale everything by the same amount. Recipes: find the amount for one person first. Speed = distance ÷ time.
examples: A recipe for 4 uses 300 g flour. How much for 6?
A cyclist rides 18 km in 1 1/2 hours. What is the speed?

cash.intro: Add up the prices, then take the total away from the money paid to find the change. Profit = money in − money spent.
examples: A comic is £2.75 and two pens are 85p each. Change from £10?
£1 = 1.25 dollars. How many pounds for 90 dollars?

time.intro: Count on in steps: to the next hour, then the hours, then the minutes. 24-hour time: 15:40 is 3:40 pm.
examples: A film starts at 3:35 pm and lasts 2 h 5 min. When does it end?

units.intro: 1 km = 1000 m, 1 m = 100 cm, 1 cm = 10 mm, 1 kg = 1000 g, 1 l = 1000 ml. Bigger to smaller unit: multiply. Smaller to bigger: divide.

eq.intro: Do the same to both sides to keep an equation balanced. In picture puzzles, find the line with only one kind of thing first.
examples: Take 4 from both sides: 8n = 88. Divide by 8: n = 11.
3 apples = 15; apple + 2 bananas = 13. What is a banana?

seq.intro: Find the rule from the gaps. If the gap is the same each time, term n = first term + (n − 1) × gap.

mach.intro: Follow the machine forwards for the output. To find the input, undo each step in reverse order.

ang.intro: Angles on a straight line add to 180°. Around a point: 360°. In a triangle: 180°. A right angle is 90°.
examples: Two angles on a line: one is 63°. The other?
A triangle has angles 50° and 53°. The third?

rect.intro: Perimeter: add all the sides (2 × length + 2 × width). Area of a rectangle: length × width, in square units.

shape.intro: Learn the properties: a square has 4 equal sides and 4 right angles; a rhombus has 4 equal sides; a trapezium has one pair of parallel sides. 3D shapes have faces, edges and vertices.
examples: How many edges does a triangular prism have?
3 on each end and 3 joining them: 9.
A cuboid is 4 × 3 × 2 cubes. How many cubes?

coord.intro: Coordinates are (across, up). In a reflection, each point moves to the same distance on the other side of the mirror line.
examples: Start at (4, 3), move 2 right and 3 up.
5 is 3 left of 8, so it goes to 3 right: (11, 4).

chart.intro: Read the scale carefully: what is each square or line worth? Add the bars to find a total.
examples: 5 children have 0 pets, 4 have 1, 3 have 2. How many pets?
A bar reaches halfway between 20 and 30. Value?

mean.intro: Mean = total ÷ how many. To find a missing value: total needed = mean × how many, then subtract what you have.
examples: Three jumps 169, 149, 159 cm. Fourth jump for a mean of 154?

wp.intro: Read the question twice, underline the numbers, decide the operation, and check the answer makes sense.
examples: Two numbers add to 64 and differ by 12.
Take the difference off: 52. Half is 26, so 26 and 38.
A mum was born in 1980 and her son in 2012. How old was she when he was born?

puz1.intro: Try small cases, look for a pattern, and check each clue. For digit puzzles, start with the last digit.
examples: A 2-digit multiple of 7 whose digits add to 12?

puz2.intro: Write what you know as a list or table. Use one fact to find the next. Check your answer fits every clue.
examples: A is twice B and B is 3 more than C. A + B + C = 41. Find C.
Win 3 points, draw 1. 8 wins and 4 draws?

count.intro: Multiply the number of choices at each step. If order does not matter, count each pair only once.
examples: 4 sandwiches and 3 drinks. How many meals?
